scenario: AITA for not staying home and taking care of my sick wife all weekend? | On Thursday evening my wife started feeling unwell. I encouraged her to go to bed and told her I could handle the kids evening stuff by myself (3 kids, ages 9, 11, and 13). I checked on her after the kids were in bed at 9 and she was fevered- I asked if she wanted any medicine, made sure she had some water, and rubbed her back for a few minutes. I slept in the spare room but got up twice to check on her. The next morning I got the kids ready and off to school, went to a meeting and came home at 10 to take her to the doctor. I worked from home until our cleaning lady came around 1 and asked her to keep an eye on my wife and went back into the office for a couple meetings, picked up the kids and was home around 4. Her fever broke shortly after I got home at 4 and I helped her shower. Our oldest had a school dance and I got some movies and set the youngest 2 up in the den for the evening with pizza and some games so they'd be quiet. I checked on my wife periodically and after the oldest got home me and the 3 kids camped out in the den. On Saturday morning, the kids were restless so I took them out for the day bc I didn't want them to be around the house being loud. I checked on my wife and she was sleeping- I refilled her water and left her a note. Throughout the day I called and sent her messages and my mom took her over some homemade soup and checked on her. We were gone the majority of the day but the kids came home worn out and we crashed in the den again. I checked on my wife as soon as we got home and she was looking better. Sunday morning, the kids and I woke up early, did some yardwork then went to the store to do the weekly grocery shopping. When we got home my wife was up and about and still weak but feeling better. However, she was being really short with me and was in a bad mood. I thought it was just bc she didn't feel well but after a few hours of her making snide comments I asked her if something was wrong and she exploded on me that her family abandoned her while she was sick. She went off about how she always takes care of us when we're sick but we avoided her like the plague and didn't stay home and I made the cleaning lady and my mom take care of her instead of doing it myself. I tried to explain that I didn't want to expose the kids to being sick and I didn't want them around the house being loud while she was trying to rest and I checked on her multiple times. She said I should've sent the kids to my parents or something and stayed home and she can't believe I didn't sleep with her for 3 days. I starting getting angry and told her that I did what I thought was best and she sounded ungrateful bc it wasn't exactly what she would've done. She then called me an asshole. We went to bed angry and didn't really speak this morning. I keep stewing over this bc I don't think that I'm an asshole but maybe I am?

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

It’s great that you feel confident when wearing a suit and tie—that’s a powerful connection between personal style and self-perception! Here’s why it might resonate with you and how to lean into it: 1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues**: Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that formal attire can subtly influence your posture, demeanor, and even hormone levels (boosting testosterone/confidence, lowering cortisol). When you feel "put together," it often *is* reflected in how you carry yourself. 2. **Social Scripts**: Suits and ties are traditionally associated with authority, professionalism, and respect—so wearing them can signal to others (and yourself) that you’re prepared, capable, and worthy of attention. This can create a feedback loop of confidence. 3. **Personal Ritual**: The act of dressing formally might feel like a *ritual of readiness*—a way to mentally transition into a mindset of competence or ambition. That’s a valuable psychological tool! 4. **Context Matters**: If you’re in an environment where suits are expected (e.g., corporate settings, formal events), they can help you blend in and feel more at ease. Conversely, if you’re the only one in a suit, it might make you stand out in a way that feels empowering. **Tips to Amplify the Effect:** - **Own the Look**: Confidence isn’t just about the clothes—it’s about how you *move* in them. Practice standing tall, making eye contact, and speaking clearly. - **Pair with Mindset**: Pair the suit with affirmations like, *"I belong here"* or *"I’m prepared for this."* Your brain will start to associate the outfit with those beliefs. - **Experiment**: Try different styles (e.g., a sharp blazer vs. a full three-piece) to see what feels most authentic to *your* version of confidence. - **Accessories**: Add elements that reflect your personality (e.g., a bold tie, a pocket square) to make it *yours*—not just a generic "business" look. **Potential Pitfalls to Watch For:** - **Over-Reliance**: Don’t let the suit *define* your confidence—it’s a tool, not the source. Confidence comes from within, but attire can be a great amplifier. - **Comfort**: If you’re uncomfortable in the suit, it’ll show. Adjust the fit, fabric, or style until it feels like *you*. **Final Thought**: Your intuition is spot-on—when something makes you feel powerful, lean into it. Confidence is contagious, and the way you dress can be a silent (but mighty) part of how you show up in the world. What’s your favorite part about wearing a suit and tie? The way it feels, the reactions you get, or something else?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Your wife’s anger isn’t just about the *outcome* (her recovery) but the *experience* of being treated as a burden. 2. **Emotional Labor & Reciprocity (Her Perspective)** - Your wife’s frustration stems from a deep-seated expectation of **mutual care**—a dynamic many couples navigate poorly. Even if you checked on her, the *absence* of presence (e.g., sleeping in the spare room, not sitting with her) can feel like emotional neglect. This is especially true if she’s used to you being her primary support. 4. **The Kids’ Well-Being** - Your concern for the kids is valid, but the *how* matters. For example: - **Alternative**: Could you have had the kids sleep in a separate room (with a babysitter if needed) to minimize noise while still being physically present with your wife? - **Communication**: Did you explain *why* you were stepping back (e.g., "I don’t want you to catch this and get sick too")? Sometimes, framing actions as protective (not dismissive) helps. 5. **The "Asshole" Label** - Calling you an "asshole" is a **gut reaction**, not a rational assessment. It’s likely a mix of: - **Frustration**: She’s sick, tired, and feeling powerless. - **Resentment**: She may feel you’ve never reciprocated her care (even if you have). - **Fear**: She’s afraid this dynamic will continue (e.g., "He’ll always prioritize the kids over me"). - **Your anger**: You’re right to feel defensive—you *did* care for her (in your eyes). But her anger isn’t about facts; it’s about *feelings*. That’s why she exploded: she needed *validation*, not justification. --- ### **Was It Wrong? (0) or Right? (1)?** **Neither.** It was **complicated**, and both perspectives have merit. Here’s why: - **0 (Wrong)**: Because you didn’t fully meet her emotional needs. Even if you managed the household well, she needed *you*—not just a cleaning lady or a note. Her anger isn’t about the weekend; it’s about feeling *seen* in her vulnerability. - **1 (Right)**: Because you balanced practical needs (kids, work, her health) and took steps to protect the family. Your wife’s criticism might be unfairly harsh, but it’s rooted in a real desire for connection. --- ### **What’s Missing?** The **emotional bridge**. Care isn’t just about *doing* things; it’s about *being present*. Your wife needed: 1. **Physical closeness**: Even if she was sleeping, sitting with her (even silently) would’ve signaled, *"I’m here for you."* 2. **Emotional validation**: A simple *"I know this sucks, and I’m here"* would’ve softened the "abandoned" feeling. 3. **Reciprocity**: She may not realize you *also* handle stress (work, kids) daily. Acknowledging that ("I know you take care of us, and I’m trying to do the same") could’ve eased tension. --- ### **How to Move Forward** 1. **Apologize for the *feeling* of abandonment** (not the actions): *"I hear how lonely and overwhelmed you felt this weekend. I didn’t realize how much you needed me to just sit with you, even if I couldn’t fix everything. I’m sorry I made you feel like you were alone in this."* (This validates her emotions without admitting fault for your choices.) 2. **Repair the trust**: - Next time she’s sick, **stay with her** (even if it’s just holding her hand or watching a movie with her). - **Delegate differently**: Ask a friend/family member to help with the kids so you can focus on her. 3. **Address the deeper issue**: - Couples often have an **unspoken contract** about care. If she’s used to being the primary caregiver, she may expect the same from you. Discuss: *"I want to be more present for you when you’re sick. How can I do that in a way that feels right for both of us?"* 4. **Reframe the "asshole" moment**: - Her anger was about *her* pain, not your character. When she calms down, say: *"I know you were hurt, and I’m sorry you felt that way. I didn’t mean to make you feel abandoned."* --- ### **Final Thought** You’re not an asshole—you’re a **human** trying to balance impossible demands (work, kids, care). But love isn’t just about *doing*; it’s about *being there*. Your wife’s reaction isn’t about the weekend; it’s about feeling **cherished**, not just *managed*. Would it help to brainstorm specific ways to show up for her next time? Or are you more focused on repairing the current tension?
